newsitem.title: INDIA: India gilts auction seen under-subscribed.
newsitem.headline: India gilts auction seen under-subscribed.

text.p: The Indian central bank's auction of government securities next week faces little chance of full subscription because of tightening money market conditions and poor timing, dealers said.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) conducts a 20 billion rupee ($560 million) auction of six-year government of India stock on Tuesday.
A Reuters poll of money market dealers showed initial subscription expected at about 50 percent with a yield of around 13.75 percent.
Subscription is seen rising to 75 percent with a yield of 13.82 percent.
The cut-off yield on five-year stock issued earlier this year was 13.75 percent while 10-year paper fetched 13.85.
"Logically, it should be closer to 13.75 percent but market expectations point to a yield of 13.80 percent or slightly above," one dealer at a foreign bank said late on Saturday.

Dealers said the RBI showed poor judgment by making the auction at a time when the call money market was showing signs of tightening and market participants were worried about liquidity over the next few months.
"Call money has tightened after about two months," a dealer at a state-run bank said. "It is not clear whether this is a temporary phase or the beginning of tighter money conditions."
Call money was quoted around 10 percent on Saturday after remaining under 5.0 percent in the last two months.
"Banks wouldn't like to lock up money, particularly in six-year paper," the dealer said.
Bankers were also surprised the auction was being held at the beginning of a fortnight when there were substantial outflows of funds from banks.
Advance tax payments by companies, which had to be made before September 15, are likely to drain around 60 billion rupees from banks into the government's coffers, they said.
Another 12.5 billion rupees will be sucked away on September 24 as instalment towards partly paid stock issued in July, dealers said.
While a yield higher than 13.80 percent could attract greater response, it was unlikely the central bank would set a higher cut-off, dealers said.

"The RBI and the finance ministry have both stated in recent times that interest rates need to be brought down," a dealer said. "Therefore, it is likely that the cut-off will be between 13.75 and 13.80 percent."
However some dealers said the RBI could pull off a surprise and set the yield higher than 13.80 percent.

"In July when a two-year stock was issued, a yield of 13.60 percent had been expected by most market participants," a dealer said. "The RBI however set a cut-off of 13.62 and several bidders were taken by surprise.
"It may do the same again... it all depends how badly the government needs the money."
